# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–32 (Complete – Updated 2026-10-13)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: Winter of eighth year after Waterloo (1830). Events span from evening of Tuesday following Fisker's departure on Saturday, 19th April through Whitsun week visit to Carbury Manor (arriving 20th May).
- **Key Locations**: London (Welbeck Street, Grosvenor Square, Abchurch Lane, Beargarden Club, Langham Hotel, Euston Square Railway Station, Bruton Street, Lincoln's Inn); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Coldcombe and Mirecombe farms; Bryngate; Pumpernickel; Ostend; Hampshire ("the Evergreens"); Brussels; Aix-la-Chapelle; Bath and Cheltenham; Carbury Hall; Carbury Chase; Caversham; Sussex; Quenwick; Dunholt village; Salford; various American locations; Suffolk.

## Major Deaths
- **John Sedley**: Died peacefully; buried at Brompton.
- **Mr. Osborne**: Deceased (four days after stroke); Major Dobbin appointed executor; Georgy established as heir.
- **Joseph Sedley**: Died at Aix-la-Chapelle three months after Dobbin's final visit. Heavily insured (£2,000); legacy split equally between Amelia and Rebecca (administratrix).
- **Colonel Rawdon Crawley**: Died of yellow fever at Coventry Island; estate devolved upon Sir Pitt's son, now Sir Rawdon Crawley, Bart.
- **Sir Pitt**: Died six weeks after Colonel Rawdon.

## Rebecca's Arc
**Seduction and Enslavement of Jos Sedley**: At Pumpernickel, Rebecca (Madame de Raudon, formerly with Rawdon Crawley) seduced Jos through calculated performance. Led him to Room No. 92, Elephant lodging-house. Jos became her "entirely slave." Lived in Brussels hotel in genteel manner. Jos died three months later at Aix-la-Chapelle. Insurance company challenged £2,000 payment; Rebecca prevailed. **Dobbin sent back his share and rigidly declined communication.**

**Final State**: Never became Lady Crawley though styles herself so. Son (Sir Rawdon, young baronet) declines to see her; receives liberal allowance. Appears very wealthy. Chiefly at Bath and Cheltenham; strong party considers her "most injured woman." Busies herself in piety, church attendance, Charity Lists.

## Amelia and William Dobbin
**Resolution**: At Ostend, Becky revealed George Osborne was "selfish humbug, low-bred cockney dandy" who wanted her to run away with him—"Dobbin forced him to keep his word." Emmy's internal struggle resolved: "There is nothing to forbid me now...I may love him with all my heart now."

**Marriage and Life**: Two mornings later at Dike, Amelia went to Dobbin "in dripping white bonnet and shawl...kissing one of his hands with all her might." Only Georgy and Jos present. Emmy told William: "Never speak of that day again." Dobbin quit service immediately, rented "the Evergreens" (Hampshire). Devoted father; fonder of daughter Jane (christened by Rev. James Crawley) than of his History of the Punjaub. Lady Jane godmother to daughter; they became great friends.

## Lady Carbury and Family

**Lady Carbury**: Lives modestly on Welbeck Street with son Felix and daughter Henrietta. "The woman was false from head to foot, but there was much of good in her, false though she was." Devoted to children, especially Felix. Descended country to Dunholt village near Carbury Manor to escape eternal parties.

**Literary Work**: Authored "Criminal Queens"—work pandering to bad tastes through fabricated crime. Crushed by "Evening Pulpit" review by Mr. Jones (Mr. Alf's reviewer); praised by "Morning Breakfast Table" review by Mr. Broune. **Mr. Alf states he never writes reviews himself; when judgment hostile to personal friend, he laments "accident" and urges friend divide him as individual from newspaper editor. Lady Carbury disbelieves, correctly suspecting Mr. Jones took direct orders from Alf.**

**Felix Carbury** (son): Beautiful as a star; cynosure of mother's eyes. Mother spoilt him; almost proud of his vices. Won £2,000 from Lord Grasslough and £400 from Miles Grendall at gaming. **Considering courtship of Marie Melmotte (great heiress); studies words ("I do") to convince her he could love her. Since Roger's offer to Henrietta, Felix "gone on from bad to worse, till his condition had become one of hopeless embarrassment." Herr Vossner convened second conference with Lords (Nidderdale and Grasslough), Miles Grendall, Sir Felix, and Paul Montague. Miles undertook to pay Vossner £450 at three months' end, endorsed by both lords, Sir Felix, and Montague. In return, Vossner produced £322 10s. in notes and gold. Felix became Director of South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway Company. Arrived at Carbury by evening mail around 4 a.m. Sunday (having failed afternoon trains Saturday, caught evening mail from distant town, posted to Carbury). Made no apology for disruption. Lied to Roger about attending Board meeting (no Board occurred; Melmotte in country). Roger considered him "miserable cub" and "cur" destined to be "hung." Felix had breakfast in bed Sunday, went to church window to smoke cigar, then asked Roger for horse to ride to Caversham afternoon.**

**Whitsun Week Visit (Chapters 31–32)**: **Lady Carbury came to Carbury Manor partly to escape eternal parties but chiefly to position Felix near Marie Melmotte (Caversham nearby). Felix promised to arrive Saturday, depart Monday. Roger Carbury prepared ladies' rooms, particularly the smaller white-hangings room (sweet with May flowers) for Henrietta, placing white rose from hot-house on dressing table. Received invitation to dinner at Caversham (Monday) from Lady Pomona Melmotte.**

**Roger's Realization and Reproach (Chapter 32)**: **Roger came to understand Lady Carbury had used his house and hospitality to further Felix's suit with Melmotte's daughter. In garden conversation, expressed disapproval of Melmotte as "dirt in the gutter," calling him adventurer and swindler. Stated: "Had it gone on in London I should have said nothing...When I am told that the girl is in the neighbourhood...and that Felix is coming here in order that he may be near to his prey, and when I am asked to be a party to the thing, I can only say what I think."**

**Lady Carbury's Response and Scheme (Chapter 32)**: **Stricken by Roger's harsh words but prepared to fight in defence of Felix. "If she did not defend him, who would?" Roger, feeling "over hot," begged pardon at garden door. She smiled but it was not one of forgiveness. Later, alone with Henrietta, Lady Carbury proposed scheme: suggested if Henrietta married Roger, his name, title, and property could go to Felix. Henrietta, understanding "tortuous mazes of manoeuvres in which her mother's mind had learned to work," disliked and almost despised them but refrained from rebukes, feeling duty to abstain.**

**Dinner Party (Chapter 32)**: **Evening party at Carbury: bishop and wife (Mrs. Yeld), Hepworths of Eardly, Father John Barham (Beccles priest). Eight guests total. Roger meticulously arranged comfort; introduced young priest first to bishop and wife, then to cousins. No mistress present; Mr. Hepworth faced Roger; bishop and priest opposite each other; ladies at four corners. Lady Carbury all smiles and pleasantness despite heart "sore with many troubles." Sat between bishop and Roger. Skilful conversation with both.**

**Mrs. Yeld's Discomfort**: Mrs. Yeld somewhat afraid of Father Barham; stauncher Protestant than bishop; uncertain whether expedient to have much to do with Roman Catholic priest. Misgivings about Catholics though bishop declared willingness to meet priest.

**Father John Barham**: Dogmatic Catholic priest. "To him it was everything that a man should believe and obey,--that he should abandon his own reason to the care of another or of others." Faith sufficient unto itself; moral conduct testimony of faith. Dogmas real religion; teaches "in season and out of season," afraid of no enemy. Single duty: bringing world to his faith. Makes approaches very gradually; tacit humility at beginning proportionate to enthusiastic volubility of advanced intimacy. At dinner, meek and agreeable with Mrs. Yeld regarding Beccles poor; had plan to induce mass said regularly in bishop's palace but did not initiate it. Alluded to "our people's" superior church attendance; Mrs. Yeld changed subject to rain. Later discussed morality of Beccles with bishop, asserting "his people" more moral than others though poorer. Named Catholic families in county (A—s, B—s, C—s, D—s); proud of their fidelity; viewed them as "salt of the earth" to restore England. Though in county only twelve months, knew nearly every Roman Catholic's name within borders. When bishop discussed old creed remaining with poor after abandoned by rich, Barham engaged Hepworth in continued argument about analogy.

**Church Attendance Sunday (Chapter 32)**: **All attended except Felix. Lady Carbury always attended church when in country, never in London—one of moral habits like early dinners and long walks. Fancied bishop would know if she failed to attend and would be displeased. Liked bishops generally; aware of woman's duty to sacrifice for society. Never in life occurred to her to think of church's purpose. On return found Felix smoking cigar on gravel path before drawing-room window.**

**Felix's Attitude**: Expressed disdain for "fellow who is always thinking of little grievances," declaring such men expect you "to go like clockwork." Resolved to ask Roger for horse as he would anyone else, unconcerned whether Roger liked it or not.

**Dinner Arrangements**: Roger received two letters. One from Lady Pomona inviting him and Henrietta to dine at Caversham on Monday. Roger expressed regret at declining (thinking how delightful if Henrietta remained, how objectionable if taken to meet Melmottes). Lady Carbury responded accepting invitation for herself, Felix, and Henrietta with great pleasure.

**Henrietta Carbury**: Romance with cousin Roger Carbury (nearly forty) and Paul Montague. Roger offered hand passionately. Paul fell in love during second visit to Carbury Hall. Hot-worded scene between Roger and Paul lasted above an hour; Paul packed and departed in tears. Roger blessed him at platform. **Henrietta rejected Roger's suit, claiming too young and age disparity insurmountable; admitted "even that disparity was not now her strongest reason." Within week, Paul returned "as a still dear friend," having promised not to see Henrietta for three months but nothing further. Wore rose from Roger's room on her bosom. When met Roger at door after garden confrontation with Lady Carbury, there was "more in her eyes of graciousness towards him than he had ever seen there before." Now watches him throughout evening, noting his courtesy as host, and thinks of mother's words that he will die wifeless and childless.**

## The Melmottes

**Augustus Melmotte**: Arrived London from Paris within two years; previously M. Melmotte. Claims English birth though speaks with accent betraying "long expatriation." In City, his name "worth any money." Big man with large whiskers, rough hair, expression of mental power on harsh vulgar face. Magnificent in expenditure, successful in business. **Miles Grendall serves as usher/secretary in office. Chairman of South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway Company with two million dollars of shares allocated to himself. Taken up old Longestaffe's affairs. Has Caversham property and old Sussex property. In country during Whitsun week; no Board meeting possible. Invited Roger and Henrietta to dinner Monday at Caversham.**

**Madame Melmotte**: Said Bohemian Jewess; speaks very little English.

**Marie Melmotte**: Speaks English well as foreigner. **Has begun forming own opinions; absolutely rejected Lord Grasslough (bankrupt, no income, ugly, vicious, ill-tempered). Had experience with Lord Nidderdale. People saying if Sir Felix Carbury managed affairs well he might be the happy man. Felix's pursuit is active; watches him waltz, observes whispering and cool effrontery, her own timid face and nervous twitching.**

## South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway Scheme

**The Enterprise**: Railway from Salt Lake City, branching from San Francisco and Chicago line, passing through New Mexico and Arizona into Mexico, terminating at Vera Cruz. Distance approximately 2,000 miles. Fisker considers cost questions "beside the mark and childish." Concession obtained from United States Government; correspondence maintained with President of Mexican Republic.

**Financial Strategy**: Stock at par; shares sold at premium to "run them up even to 110," yielding three hundred thousand dollars minimum. Directors understood fortune made by floating shares, not making actual railway.

**London Directorate**: Company fully launched with Melmotte (chairman), Lord Alfred Grendall, Sir Felix Carbury, Samuel Cohenlupe (Member of Parliament for Staines, Jewish persuasion), Lord Nidderdale, and Paul Montague.

**Fisker's Departure**: Started Saturday morning, 19th April. Met at railway station by Nidderdale and Montague.

**Paul Montague**: Junior member of firm. English. Personally dislikes Fisker but unable to resist his combination. Trembles for his money. Met Fisker at Liverpool; Fisker displayed maps, schedules, programmes. Letter from Langham Hotel invited Melmotte to meet. Paul and Fisker travelled to London together next morning. Paul living at Beargarden; entertained Lord Alfred once; dined twice with Melmotte in Grosvenor Square. Fisker suggested Paul enter for "great Marie Melmotte plate." **Saw good deal of Sir Felix, Lord Nidderdale; champagne consumption increased. Could not wake up on London mornings with satisfactory thoughts as at Carbury Hall. At Beargarden cardroom, offered to undertake Grendall's debt himself; disallowed.**

## Roger Carbury
Nearly forty years old. Never owed shilling he could not pay; father likewise. Carbury parish named for family. Carbury Chase unfortunately belongs entirely to Bundlesham estate. Remains firmly opposed to Melmotte connection on principle; holds old-fashioned idea that "touching of pitch will defile." Took degree at Oxford; became what called "pervert," supposed "convert." Works as priest earning approximately day-labourer's wages, forced to buy second-hand clothes. Described as "certainly...a gentleman." Soft heart; knows Lady Carbury false and Felix worthless, yet utterly condemns himself for harsh words. Prepared apology when met Henrietta at door after garden confrontation.

## The Longestaffes

**Sir Merton Longestaffe**: Owns properties in Sussex and Caversham. **Determined no more London expenses that year, announcing family will not return to London from Caversham. Desires to sell Pickering and disembarrass Caversham from debt. Dolly refused to consent unless half produce given to him for his own mortgaged estate; consequence: Pickering could not be sold.**

**Georgiana Longestaffe**: **Strong-minded protest against Melmottes; threatened to stay in London rather than be "buried" at Caversham.**

**Adolphus (Dolly) Longestaffe**: Has rooms own in Bruton Street; seldom dines with family. Obdurate regarding his own rights in property dealings with father.
